  `554.83 ms` model_total and `452.67 ms` audio_head. The extra branch/helper
  did not reduce the real queued-work/readback cost enough to justify keeping.
- Phase result: tuned the default LFM2.5 ASR stop-check interval from `96` to
  `92`, preserving the one-read chunked path for the diarization benchmark
  while avoiding four speculative device decode forwards. Full ASR warmup
  preserved `gen_tokens=91`, reduced `dev_argmax` to `92`, and improved
  model_total to `1152.88 ms` with RTF `0.042`. TTS guard stayed effectively
  neutral/noisy (`542.58 ms` avg model_total, `536.78 ms` p50, same
  token/frame invariants).
- Phase result: added a greedy final-TTS chunked audio stop-check path that
  keeps sampled codebooks device-side for main audio embedding, checks first
  codebook stop tokens every `20` frames, and sends stacked device code tensors
  directly into the detokenizer. Full TTS warmup improved versus the prior
  committed guard to `505.19 ms` model_total, `317.86 ms` audio_head,
  `63.46 ms` materialization, and preserved user-visible audio shape
  (`39` frames, `3.12 s`, `40` audio-head calls). Logical `gen_tokens`/text
  sample counts moved from `42`/`2` to `41`/`1` because final TTS now stops at
  audio EOS instead of sampling the post-audio text transition. ASR guard stayed
  in band (`1130.37 ms` model_total, `91` gen tokens, `92` device argmax).
  Interval sweeps rejected `16` because it speculated to `48` audio-head calls;
  `10` preserved `40` calls but was slightly slower than `20`.

# LFM2.5 Audio Metal/CPU Performance Investigation

## Goal
Investigate Metal/CPU-specific kernel opportunities in the Rust/Candle
implementation of `LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B-GGUF`, then produce benchmark goals for
future implementation. This is research and planning only; no product-code
changes.

## Plan
- [x] Review project lessons and current benchmark evidence.
- [x] Map LFM2.5 TTS and ASR hot stages to source files and Candle operations.
- [x] Inspect current Metal/CPU optimization hooks, custom ops, and telemetry.
- [x] Cross-check Candle Metal/CPU capabilities and constraints from primary
  sources.
- [x] Rank candidate kernel work by expected impact, risk, and verification
  needs.
- [x] Define benchmark goals for TTS and ASR under Metal/CPU.
- [x] Document findings, review notes, and verification limits here.

## Review
- Scope stayed research/planning-only. Product code was not edited. Evidence came
  from source inspection, locked Candle 0.10.2 sources, local GGUF metadata, and
  read-only subagent passes for TTS, ASR, and backend/kernel infrastructure.
- TTS routing lands in
  `Lfm25AudioModel::generate_sequential_with_config_and_callback`. The reported
  hot buckets map to main prefill, per-frame audio-head/depthformer generation,
  and detokenizer decode/ISTFT. `main_backbone` is a broad wrapper that includes
  `audio_head`, so those numbers should not be added together.
- ASR routing lands in `Lfm25AudioModel::transcribe_to_output_with_callback`.
  The strongest finding is the decode-loop synchronization: current Metal
  greedy argmax still materializes a host scalar per token. Candle's Metal
  `to_cpu` path performs a blit and `wait_until_completed`, matching the
  benchmark shape where `decode=761.69 ms` and the LFM sampling/scalar-read
  proxy accounts for `711.08 ms` while `loop_fwd` is only `48.69 ms`.
- Existing LFM Metal work is real: quantized projections use Candle `QMatMul`,
  MLP SiLU-mul, q/k RMS norm, RoPE pair, and single-token decode GQA already
  have fused paths. Runtime counters also show fused attention and RoPE success
  for the supplied runs. The next gains are mostly removing host syncs and
  adding sequence-prefill/audio/conformer kernels, not starting from zero.
- Highest-impact candidate: keep ASR next-token selection on device and feed the
  device argmax tensor directly into the next decode step. Read generated IDs in
  chunks or at the end, with an explicit EOS/stop-token strategy. This is the
  first target because it attacks the largest isolated waste in the supplied ASR
  benchmark.
- Second candidate: enable the shared Metal SDPA path for LFM main sequence
  prefill where a pure causal attention path can be used. LFM currently uses the
  shared helper for CUDA prefill and a custom Metal decode kernel, while Metal
  sequence prefill falls through to matmul/mask/softmax/matmul. Masked/sliding
  cases need more care because shared masked Metal SDPA is off by default and
  only accepts rank-4 F16/BF16 masks.
- Third candidate: add LFM shortconv kernels. The local GGUF metadata shows the
  main model has 16 layers with only 6 attention layers and 10 shortconv layers;
  the tokenizer/detokenizer backbone has 8 layers with 5 shortconv layers. A
  fused Metal and CPU path for l_cache=3 shortconv/gating should reduce
  prefill, decode-forward overhead, and detokenizer backbone cost.
- Fourth candidate: optimize TTS audio-head depthformer sampling. The benchmark
  spends about `496 ms` there for roughly 39 audio frames. Opportunities include
  keeping codebook samples on device between greedy selection and audio-frame
  embedding, reducing per-frame cache/workspace allocation, and fusing small
  depthformer/logit operations that currently dispatch many tiny kernels.
- Fifth candidate: split and optimize detokenizer. The current `129 ms` includes
  codebook embedding/upsample, an 8-layer LFM backbone, projection, Metal-to-CPU
  spectrogram copy, and CPU RustFFT ISTFT/overlap-add. Add substage telemetry
  first, then target CPU vectorization/parallel overlap-add or a later Metal
  ISTFT path.
- Sixth candidate: Conformer encoder kernels for ASR. The `696 ms` encoder path
  is real and uses Conv2d subsampling, 17 Conformer layers, relative-position
  attention, depthwise Conv1d, and adapter projection. Low-risk work is caching
  relative-position embeddings; larger work is reusing/paralleling the existing
  Parakeet Metal depthwise convolution patterns and eventually fusing
  relative-position attention.
- CPU-specific work should start with a CPU baseline for the same commands. The
  most plausible CPU wins are l_cache=3 shortconv, detokenizer ISTFT/overlap-add,
  Conformer conv/activation fusion, and avoiding unnecessary tensor creation.
  The ASR per-token Metal scalar-read issue is not expected to transfer directly
  to CPU because CPU argmax is already host-resident.
- Phase 0 benchmark goal: add better LFM telemetry with no behavior change.
  Targets are no more than +/-2% model-total movement, identical or expected
  token/frame counts, and new splits for ASR argmax vs host read, TTS audio-head
  substeps, detokenizer backbone/copy/ISTFT, and LFM fused-kernel hit/fallbacks.
- Phase 1 Metal goals: TTS model_total `<=1250-1350 ms`, RTF `<=0.43`,
  tokens/sec `>=31`; ASR model_total `<=1850-2050 ms`, decode `<=150-220 ms`,
  LFM sampling/scalar-read proxy `<=60-100 ms`, RTF `<=0.075`.
- Phase 2 Metal goals: TTS model_total `<=950-1100 ms`, RTF `<=0.34`,
  tokens/sec `>=38-42`; ASR model_total `<=1450-1650 ms`, encoder
  `<=575-620 ms`, prefill `<=750-900 ms`, decode `<=100-150 ms`, RTF
  `<=0.055-0.060`.
- Stretch goals after deeper kernels: TTS model_total `<=750-900 ms`, audio_head
  `<=220-260 ms`, detokenizer `<=50-70 ms`; ASR model_total `<=1100-1300 ms`,
  encoder `<=450-520 ms`, prefill `<=600-750 ms`, decode `<=80-120 ms`.
- Verification plan for implementation: repeat the exact warmup benchmark
  commands, track avg/p50/p95 and stage timings, compare output correctness
  against baseline transcripts/audio duration/token counts, run with fused
  kernels enabled/disabled where applicable, and add CPU baselines before
  assigning absolute CPU millisecond targets.

# Voice AI Runtime Architecture Gap Analysis

## Goal
Read `docs/dev/Voice-AI-Inference-Runtime.md`, compare its proposed
model-agnostic voice AI runtime architecture against the current source tree,
and produce a staged research/planning summary of what is done, partial, and
still needed. This is research and planning only; no product-code changes.

## Plan
- [x] Review project lessons and task-management constraints.
- [x] Read the reference architecture end to end and extract the comparison
  dimensions.
- [x] Inventory current code for API/control-plane, data-plane/media,
  model-registry/runtime, jobs/sessions, governance, and observability evidence.
- [x] Compare code evidence against the proposed architecture and classify each
  area as done, partial, or missing.
- [x] Group remaining work into staged implementation phases.
- [x] Document the review, evidence, verification limits, and staged plan here.

## Review
- Started as a research/planning-only task. Product code should not be edited.
- Existing lessons reviewed. Relevant constraints: source files are the
  authority for architecture claims, `tasks/*` should stay local-only unless
  explicitly requested, and documented promises must be checked against literal
  implementation wiring.
- Verification method: static source inspection plus read-only subagent passes
  for control plane, data plane, and model/runtime/governance. No tests or
  server smoke runs were needed because this was not a behavior-change task.
- Overall verdict: Izwi has a substantial local voice inference runtime, not a
  thin prototype. It is most aligned with the doc at the model-loader,
  local-execution, OpenAI-compatible API, realtime voice, and desktop-oriented
  persistence layers. The main misalignment is architectural: the doc describes
  a model-agnostic platform with durable control-plane objects, queue-backed
  data-plane execution, first-class artifacts, tenant-aware governance, model
  deployments, webhooks, and compliance/provenance. The current implementation
  is still mostly a local monolith with route-specific records and several
  scaffolded future boundaries.

### Done Or Substantially Implemented
- API surface: the Axum router exposes `/v1`, health/readiness, OpenAPI/docs,
  internal metrics, first-party media/transcription/diarization/speech/voice
  routes, and OpenAI-compatible audio/chat/models/responses routes
  (`crates/izwi-server/src/api/router.rs`, `api/openai/mod.rs`).
- Synchronous and streaming speech APIs: OpenAI-style transcription and speech
  endpoints support uploaded audio, response formats, TTS streaming events,
  saved voices/reference audio checks, and runtime semaphore protection
  (`api/openai/audio/transcriptions.rs`, `api/openai/audio/speech.rs`).
- Persisted speech-text records: first-party `/v1/speech-to-text/jobs` creates
  pending records, stores uploaded audio, spawns processing, updates progress,
  stores outputs, and exposes list/get/delete/rerun/cancel surfaces where the
  underlying route supports them (`api/transcription/mod.rs`,
  `api/transcription/handlers.rs`, `api/transcription/unified_write.rs`).
- Realtime voice primitives: voice WebSocket flow implements VAD, endpointing,
  utterance finalization, modular ASR->agent->TTS and unified audio-chat turns,
  interruption/barge-in, and persisted voice sessions/turns
  (`app/voice_realtime.rs`, `voice_store.rs`). Realtime transcription also
  exists as rolling-buffer WebSocket inference (`app/transcription_realtime.rs`).
- Local media/audio primitives: media upload and route-specific stores persist
  bytes through local/provider storage; audio payload helpers inspect sample
  rate, duration, channels, RMS/peak/clipping; core has decode/resampling/VAD
  and ASR chunking/stitching primitives (`api/media/handlers.rs`,
  `api/audio_payload.rs`, `audio/inspection.rs`, `izwi-vad`, `izwi-asr-toolkit`).
- Model/runtime foundation: a static catalog, model manager, downloader,
  residency snapshots, native model registry, CPU/Metal/CUDA backend selection,
  scheduler/KV-cache engine, capability adapter registry, and conformance
  cases exist (`catalog/metadata.rs`, `model/manager.rs`, `residency/mod.rs`,
  `runtime/adapters.rs`, `engine/*`).
- Observability baseline: request tracing, request-context audit hook calls,
  runtime latency counters, voice/broker/pipeline counters, JSON metrics, and
  Prometheus output are implemented (`api/request_context.rs`,
  `runtime/telemetry/metrics.rs`, `api/internal/metrics.rs`).

### Partial Foundations
- Control plane vs data plane: modules roughly map to control/data-plane
  responsibilities, but they run in one local server process. There is no
  durable job service, event bus, worker service, or deployment gateway.
- Jobs: transcription/diarization records are useful job-like objects, but they
  are route-specific and narrow. Statuses are mostly pending/processing/ready/
  failed; cancellation is incomplete; retries are manual or model-local; there
  is no unified job state machine, idempotency key, retry policy, or durable
  queue.
- Sessions: voice sessions/turns are persisted, but streaming state is
  connection/process-local. There is no standalone Session service with
  affinity, reconnect/resume, expiry, cache-backed buffers, or tenant/billing
  accounting.
- Assets/artifacts: media paths and output JSON/audio are stored, but there are
  no first-class MediaAsset, TextAsset, Artifact, Transcript, or Compliance
  Artifact records with stable artifact IDs, checksum, scan state, lifecycle,
  retention, provenance, or intermediate outputs.
- Routing and task graphs: the capability adapters, broker, residency, and
  pipeline graph contracts are valuable scaffolding. Several comments explicitly
  state they are metadata-first or inert; existing execution still follows
  route/runtime-specific paths rather than a broker-selected deployment or
  retryable task graph (`runtime/broker.rs`, `runtime/pipeline.rs`).
- Governance hooks: `izwi-hooks` defines auth, policy, audit, data governance,
  model artifact policy, observability, quota, secret, admin workflow, database,
  and media-storage extension points. In the inspected OSS server/core, only
  HTTP auth/policy and request audit are materially wired; quotas, model
  artifact policy, inference governance, data retention, and admin workflow
  enforcement are not generally called.
- Model registry: the catalog exposes model IDs, licenses, status, local paths,
  speech capabilities, route capabilities, and CUDA metadata. It is not the
  doc's governance registry with immutable artifacts, checksums, model versions,
  approval state, evaluation results, deployment records, canaries, rollback, or
  tenant-scoped policy.
- Evaluation: CLI benchmark tooling, conformance cases, and smoke manifests
  exist, but there is no built-in evaluation platform with datasets, WER/CER
  gates, speaker-error metrics, TTS naturalness/similarity gates, human-review
  workflows, or release-blocking model gates.

### Missing Against The Proposed Architecture
- Tenant-aware baseline: users/tenants/API keys, quota/rate-limit enforcement,
  per-tenant object ownership, cost accounting, and tenant IDs on every durable
  object.
- Durable orchestration: event bus, queue, worker pools, retry/cancel/resume,
  dead-letter/error taxonomy, idempotent job creation, idempotent webhook
  delivery, and cross-process recovery.
- Public platform APIs: general job management across ASR/TTS/S2S/diarization,
  artifacts API, webhooks, model capability/deployment APIs, audit/compliance
  export APIs, and signed upload/download URLs.
- Media platform: canonical normalized audio derivatives, remote URL ingest,
  direct multipart upload/session upload, video extraction, content scanning,
  checksum/dedupe, retention, deletion cascades, and searchable transcript
  artifacts.
- Model platform: first-class ModelArtifact and ModelDeployment stores with
  source/version/checksum/runtime requirements, license/safety metadata, eval
  results, worker pool/replica/health/routing weight, aliases, canary, rollback,
  and multi-runtime execution beyond local Candle CPU/Metal/CUDA.
- Voice safety/compliance: consent ledger, voice owner/scope/revocation,
  commercial/public-figure restrictions, synthetic-media provenance,
  watermarking/labeling, redaction, and policy/audit records tied to every
  generated output.
- Production observability: per-stage traces linked by job/artifact/model
  deployment IDs, worker utilization, queue depth by stage, quality metrics,
  safety failures, cost per minute/token, tenant-level SLOs, and alerting hooks.

### Doc Roadmap Alignment
- Doc Phase 1, Batch Runtime Foundation: partially started. Local APIs,
  persisted ASR/diarization records, model loading, storage, and metrics exist.
  Durable jobs, queue-backed orchestration, generalized artifacts, quotas,
  idempotency, webhooks, and safety audit are still missing.
- Doc Phase 2, Transcript and Audio Quality: partially started. ASR chunking,
  VAD, forced alignment, diarization, summary generation, and export-oriented
  output formats exist. Canonical transcript versions, quality metrics,
  search/indexing, normalized media assets, and evaluation harnesses remain.
- Doc Phase 3, Streaming Runtime: partially started. Realtime voice and
  transcription WebSockets are real. A production Session service, affinity,
  reconnect/resume, stable partial/final/correction event contract, cache-backed
  buffers, and stream billing/quotas remain.
- Doc Phase 4, Model Platform Maturity: mostly missing beyond the local model
  catalog/manager/adapters. Artifact/deployment registry, broker-based routing,
  canary/rollback, eval gates, and policy-aware model selection remain.
- Doc Phase 5, Enterprise and Safety Maturity: mostly missing. Hook contracts
  exist, but tenant governance, quotas, consent, provenance, audit export,
  retention, and admin workflows need actual data models and enforcement.

### Staged Work Plan
- Stage 0: Freeze architecture contracts before large rewrites. Write concrete
  Rust/API specs for MediaAsset, TextAsset, Job, Session, Artifact,
  ModelArtifact, ModelDeployment, Capability metadata, and event names. Add
  conformance tests that assert existing routes can be wrapped by those
  contracts without changing behavior.
- Stage 1: Build the batch foundation around existing routes. Add first-class
  media/text/job/artifact tables, idempotency keys, a unified job status API,
  output artifact IDs, and webhook configuration models. Wrap current
  transcription and diarization records first; add TTS jobs after the job shape
  is stable.
- Stage 2: Replace spawned route tasks with durable orchestration. Introduce a
  local queue abstraction, stage records, retry/cancel/resume semantics,
  dead-letter handling, and progress events. Use the current pipeline graph
  contracts as the stage taxonomy, but keep workers local initially.
- Stage 3: Promote media/transcript quality into platform objects. Store
  canonical normalized audio assets, chunk maps, alignment artifacts,
  transcript versions, speaker-turn artifacts, subtitle exports, and quality
  metadata. Add retention/deletion behavior before exposing broader artifact
  downloads.
- Stage 4: Turn model metadata scaffolding into a real model platform. Add
  ModelArtifact and ModelDeployment records, checksum/version/source metadata,
  license/safety/eval fields, aliases, default model policies, and deployment
  health. Then move broker routing from validation/shadow into real selection
  with fallback chains.
- Stage 5: Harden realtime sessions. Create a Session service/store for
  low-latency session metadata, affinity, reconnect/resume, expiry, stable
  event sequencing, backpressure accounting, and billing/quotas. Keep the
  existing WebSocket protocols as compatibility fronts while moving state out
  of connection structs.
- Stage 6: Implement enterprise/safety primitives. Add tenant/user/API-key
  models, quota checks, data-governance enforcement, voice consent/ownership/
  revocation, generated-audio provenance, audit ledgers, retention policies,
  deletion cascades, and compliance export APIs.
- Stage 7: Scale and evaluate. Split gateway/worker process roles, add worker
  pools/autoscaling signals, queue/worker observability, benchmark/evaluation
  datasets, WER/CER/speaker/TTS gates, canary/rollback workflows, and cost/SLO
  dashboards.

### Suggested Execution Order
- Do Stage 0 first even if it feels slow; it reduces churn by making the
  existing monolith wrap-compatible with the target runtime.
- Stages 1 and 2 are the highest leverage because many later features depend on
  durable jobs, artifacts, and stage records.
- Stages 4 and 5 can proceed in parallel after Stage 2 if ownership is split:
  one path owns model registry/routing, the other owns realtime session state.
- Stage 6 should start with data-model fields during Stages 1/4/5, but full
  enforcement should wait until the objects being governed actually exist.
- Stage 7 should be delayed until there are durable queues, deployments,
  artifacts, and evaluation outputs to measure.

# Phase 3 Streaming Runtime Implementation Plan

## Goal
Research and plan how to implement Phase 3, Streaming Runtime, from
`docs/dev/Voice-AI-Inference-Runtime.md` without breaking the existing web
application or desktop application. This is analysis and planning only; do not
edit product code.

## Plan
- [x] Review project lessons and task-management constraints.
- [x] Read the full Voice AI runtime reference document.
- [x] Extract Phase 3 requirements and dependencies on earlier phases.
- [x] Inspect current backend realtime, streaming TTS, session, metrics, and
  router code.
- [x] Inspect current UI and desktop integration points that rely on realtime
  or streaming behavior.
- [x] Identify compatibility risks, migration strategy, and verification gates.
- [x] Document the proposed implementation plan and review results here.

## Review
- This was a research/planning-only task. Product code was not edited.
- Source inspection covered the full runtime reference document, backend
  realtime and streaming routes, runtime/core streaming helpers, voice session
  persistence, telemetry, model route-capability metadata, React clients, and
  Tauri desktop startup/injection.
- Phase 3 should be treated as an internal runtime extraction first, not a
  public API replacement. The existing web and desktop apps have concrete wire
  contracts that must remain stable: `/v1/speech-to-text/realtime/ws` with
  `ITRW` PCM16 frames, `/v1/voice/realtime/ws` with `IVWS` PCM16 frames,
  `/v1/audio/speech` SSE JSON events, speech-history/transcription SSE events,
  OpenAI chat/responses streaming, the `/v1` base URL, and desktop
  `localhost:8080` startup assumptions.
- Current Phase 3 coverage is partial. Live transcription and voice WebSockets
  exist, voice VAD/endpointing and barge-in exist, streaming TTS exists for
  compatible model paths, and durable voice sessions/turns exist. Missing or
  incomplete pieces are a real Session service, reconnect/resume, stable
  partial/final/correction event semantics for live ASR, explicit stream
  cancellation/backpressure policy, streaming admission control, and actual
  recording of the richer streaming metrics already named in the metric catalog.

### Implementation Plan
- Phase 0: Freeze compatibility contracts before refactoring.
  Add tests around current event names, binary headers, SSE payload shapes,
  route status expectations, and UI URL builders. The important golden
  contracts are `ITRW` and `IVWS` frame layouts, voice event `type` strings,
  `audio.started`/`audio.chunk`/`audio.done`/`audio.failed`, transcription
  `transcript.text.delta`/`transcript.text.done`, speech-history `created`/
  `start`/`delta|chunk`/`final`/`error`/`done`, OpenAI `[DONE]`, and model
  download EventSource payloads.
- Phase 1: Add an internal streaming runtime module under existing routes.
  Introduce `StreamingSessionService`, `StreamingSessionId`,
  `StreamingSessionKind`, `SessionCommand`, `SessionEvent`,
  `SessionCancellation`, `SessionBackpressurePolicy`, and per-session timing
  snapshots. Register it in `AppState`. Keep it in-process for the first pass;
  do not add a new server process, port, or public endpoint.
- Phase 2: Move live transcription state behind the service.
  Extract `RealtimeSessionState`, native ASR stream handling, rolling-buffer
  recompute, partial merge logic, and pending inference cancellation from
  `app/transcription_realtime.rs` into a `LiveAsrSession` worker owned by the
  service. Keep the WebSocket handler as a protocol shim that still accepts
  `session_start`, `session_stop`, `ping`, and `ITRW` PCM16 frames. Add optional
  `session_id`, `event_id`, `is_final`, and timing fields only after existing
  clients continue to pass.
- Phase 3: Move voice-agent session state behind the service.
  Extract `ConnectionState`, `StreamingInputState`, VAD/endpointing, active-turn
  tracking, and turn task spawning into a `VoiceRealtimeSession` worker. Reuse
  `VoiceStore` for durable `voice_sessions`/`voice_turns`; do not repurpose
  those rows as live transport buffers. Preserve lazy durable session creation
  on `input_stream_start`, current `turn_done` statuses, barge-in behavior,
  and assistant audio `pcm_i16` binary frames.
- Phase 4: Make cancellation and backpressure explicit.
  Give every live session and active turn a cancellation handle that can abort
  ASR, chat, TTS, and unified S2S consistently. Keep current external
  `interrupt` behavior. Centralize queue capacity and policy decisions, but
  initially mimic existing behavior: bounded WebSocket outbound queues drop and
  record backpressure, core streaming defaults remain fail-on-full where they
  do today, and SSE client disconnect cancels generation.
- Phase 5: Add streaming metrics at the service boundary.
  Wire real measurements for the metrics already cataloged in
  `runtime/voice_metrics.rs`: first partial latency, ASR finalization delay,
  endpointing latency, TTS first-audio latency, barge-in latency, ingress
  dropped/stale frames, jitter, underrun/backpressure counts, active sessions,
  and session duration. Expose them through existing `/v1/internal/metrics` and
  Prometheus output without removing current fields.
- Phase 6: Improve streaming TTS through a shared audio stream adapter.
  Factor a common server-side adapter for `/audio/speech` SSE,
  speech-history streams, and voice assistant audio chunks. Keep existing event
  names and `pcm_i16` default. Model-native streaming can emit progressive
  chunks; final-only models should still emit a compatible start/chunk/final
  sequence rather than pretending to be low-latency.
- Phase 7: Add optional reconnect/resume once the service owns state.
  Add opt-in fields such as `resume_session_id` and `last_event_id` to
  `session_start`, plus bounded event replay for recent non-audio JSON events.
  Existing clients should remain free to ignore these fields and continue using
  close-to-idle behavior.
- Phase 8: Tighten streaming capability metadata.
  Keep the existing broad `speech_to_text_realtime` and `voice_realtime_*`
  route flags for UI compatibility, but add internal distinctions such as
  native streaming ASR vs rolling batch recompute, final-only TTS vs progressive
  TTS, and latency class. Route/admission decisions should use the refined
  internal metadata before the UI starts depending on it.

### Expected Code Shape
- New server module: `crates/izwi-server/src/streaming_runtime/` with
  `mod.rs`, `service.rs`, `types.rs`, `live_asr.rs`, `voice.rs`, `adapters.rs`,
  and `metrics.rs`.
- `crates/izwi-server/src/state.rs`: add
  `streaming_sessions: Arc<StreamingSessionService>`.
- `crates/izwi-server/src/app/transcription_realtime.rs`: shrink to WebSocket
  parsing/serialization and service command forwarding.
- `crates/izwi-server/src/app/voice_realtime.rs`: shrink to WebSocket
  parsing/serialization and voice protocol adapter; move turn orchestration into
  the service worker.
- `crates/izwi-core/src/runtime/telemetry/metrics.rs` and
  `crates/izwi-core/src/runtime/voice_metrics.rs`: add actual sample storage
  and recording methods for the existing Phase 3 metric names.
- `ui/src/features/voice/realtime/support.ts` and
  `ui/src/features/transcription/playground/support.ts`: only additive optional
  fields at first, such as `session_id` or `is_final`; URL builders and binary
  frame helpers should not change.
- `crates/izwi-desktop/*`: no required change if `/v1`, host, port, binary
  names, and single-process server model remain unchanged.

### Compatibility Risks
- Do not remove or rename existing event `type`/`event` strings; the UI switch
  statements depend on them.
- Do not change `ITRW` or `IVWS` binary headers; the UI encoders/parsers are
  fixed to those layouts.
- Do not switch voice assistant audio away from `pcm_i16` by default; the voice
  route currently errors on other streamed formats.
- Do not make clients provide a session ID to start; current clients only send
  `session_start` and expect the server to create state.
- Do not hold the global inference semaphore for an idle listening session; only
  hold it while inference work is actually running.
- Do not introduce a second server port, sidecar, or new desktop startup path
  for Phase 3. Desktop injects one origin and the UI appends `/v1`.
- Do not advertise OpenAI `/v1/realtime/*` support as part of this work; the
  current OpenAI compatibility contract marks those endpoints out of scope.

### Verification Gates For The Future Implementation
- Rust unit tests for frame parsing, event adapters, session state transitions,
  cancellation, backpressure counters, and voice-store persistence.
- Route/contract tests for existing WebSocket upgrade paths and SSE event
  payloads before and after extraction.
- UI tests for URL builders, optional event fields, TTS stream parsing,
  transcription stream parsing, and voice binary audio parsing.
- Local smoke matrix on a patched server: `/audio/speech` SSE, speech-history
  TTS SSE, `/audio/transcriptions` SSE, live transcription WS with synthetic
  PCM16 frames, voice realtime WS with synthetic speech/silence frames, chat
  SSE, responses SSE, and model download EventSource.
- Desktop non-regression: `cargo check -p izwi-desktop`, packaged binary still
  starts `izwi-server` on `localhost:8080`, and the webview still resolves
  `window.__IZWI_SERVER_URL__ + /v1`.
- [x] Cross-check backend/kernel/serving claims against implementation
  evidence.
- [x] Summarize missing capabilities and likely priority order.
- [x] Add review notes and verification limits.

# Phase 3 Streaming Runtime Implementation

## Goal
Implement the Phase 3 Streaming Runtime plan without breaking the existing web
or desktop applications. Commit each phase separately after verification.

## Plan
- [x] Phase 0: Freeze existing streaming/realtime compatibility contracts with
  executable tests.

# Qwen3 TTS Ambitious Metal/CPU Performance Implementation

## Goal
Achieve the ambitious Qwen3 TTS performance targets for
`Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-0.6B-CustomVoice` and
`Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-CustomVoice` while preserving CPU/Metal correctness and
keeping at most one local `izwi-server` process active at a time.

Primary 0.6B Metal fox-sentence targets from the current baseline:
- Average wall/server generation <= 4500 ms.
- Decode <= 3300 ms.
- Tokens/sec >= 60.
- RTF <= 1.50.

Relative targets until fresh baselines exist:
- CPU: phase-B average latency improvement >= 15-20%.
- 1.7B Metal: phase-B average latency improvement >= 30-35%, stretch
  >= 40-45%.

## Plan
- [x] Phase 0: Add deterministic benchmark controls and Qwen3 TTS component
  diagnostics/timers so CPU/Metal kernel changes can be measured cleanly;
  verify without running more than one server; commit.
- [x] Phase 1: Wire existing Metal fused SiLU-mul into Qwen3 TTS talker and
  predictor MLPs; verify unit/compile checks and targeted benchmark smoke;
  commit if faster or neutral with counters proving use.
- [x] Phase 2: Wire existing Metal fused Q/K RMSNorm and cached/fused RoPE
  into Qwen3 TTS talker and predictor single-token decode; verify correctness
  and telemetry counters; commit if faster or neutral with lower dispatch cost.
- [x] Phase 3: Add a dense/head-major decode-cache path for TTS talker and
  predictor on eligible non-quantized Metal, using the existing single-token
  GQA Metal decode kernel with paged KV fallback; verify and commit.
- [x] Phase 4: Add CPU contiguous single-token GQA attention and sampling/
  argmax cleanup where profiling shows measurable host-side overhead; verify
  and commit.
- [x] Phase 5: Run final benchmark matrix under the one-server policy for
  0.6B CPU/Metal and 1.7B CPU/Metal where hardware memory allows; document
  targets met/missed honestly.
- [x] Phase 6: Remove avoidable single-token embedding gather/allocation work
  from Qwen3 TTS talker/predictor decode loops; verify equivalence, benchmark
  under the one-server policy, and commit only if faster or neutral.
- [x] Phase 7: Remove avoidable final audio-buffer copies from the
  non-streaming Qwen TTS executor/API response path; verify response encoding
  and release build; commit.
- [x] Phase 8: Add human-readable TTS diagnostics component summaries to the
  benchmark CLI so future Qwen TTS kernel/cache experiments are easier to
  compare; verify and commit.
- [x] Phase 9: Avoid duplicate final speech-tokenizer decode in direct
  non-streaming Qwen TTS helper APIs; verify core tests and commit.
- [x] Phase 10: Move owned Qwen TTS decode-step samples in the executor instead
  of copying them into final output buffers; verify and commit.
- [x] Phase 11: Test predictor open-page cache reuse across per-frame clears;
  reject after Metal A/B regression and document.
- [x] Phase 20: Add paged decode attention shape and optional phase-timing
  telemetry so the next Metal/CPU kernel attempt can target measured hot
  substeps; verify and commit.
- [x] Phase 21: Run a bounded Metal paged-decode profile with
  `IZWI_PAGED_DECODE_PROFILE=1`, choose the highest-impact paged-attention
  substep, implement the next kernel/cache optimization, verify, document, and
  commit.
- [x] Phase 22: Run a 3-iteration 96-token Metal validation benchmark for the
  kept single-page GQA fast path, document whether it remains a normalized win,
  and commit the documentation phase.

- Lessons reviewed: keep dense KV cache growth bounded on memory-constrained

  paged profiles both averaged one page per paged decode call, so the patch
  targets the single-page case by routing compatible dense pages through the
  existing fused decode-GQA Metal kernel. Verification passed:
  - `cargo test -p izwi-core test_single_page_gqa_fast_path_returns_none_on_cpu -- --nocapture`
  - `cargo test -p izwi-core test_grouped_paged_decode_matches_single_page_loop -- --nocapture`
  - `cargo test -p izwi-cli kernel_path_telemetry_deserializes_flash_fallback_reasons -- --nocapture`
  - `cargo check -p izwi-core -p izwi-server -p izwi-cli`
  - `cargo build --release -p izwi-server -p izwi-cli`
  Candidate 0.6B Metal 96-token smoke: 15386.1 ms, 47.33 tokens/sec,
  RTF 1.981, 7.68s audio, 8260 / 8260 / 0 single-page GQA
  attempt/success/fallback. Kill-switch control: 8416.0 ms, 33.98 tokens/sec,
  RTF 2.759, 3.04s audio, 0 / 0 / 0 fast-path counters. Decision is based on
  normalized tokens/sec/RTF because clip lengths differed.
- Phase 22 result: reject the single-page GQA fast path as default-on after
  fuller validation. The 3-iteration 96-token Metal run reached 22262.2 ms
  average, 32.42 tokens/sec, RTF 2.897, 7.68s average audio, WAV valid, with
  24780 / 24780 / 0 fast-path attempt/success/fallback. This regresses below
  the kept acoustic-embedding-sum baseline, so the code is now opt-in with
  `IZWI_PAGED_DECODE_SINGLE_PAGE_GQA=1`. The server was stopped after the run.

# Qwen3 TTS Metal/CPU Kernel Opportunity Research

## Goal
Investigate where `Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-0.6B-CustomVoice` and
`Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-CustomVoice` can benefit from Candle Metal and CPU kernel
work, then propose benchmark goals for future implementation. This is a
research, analysis, and planning task only.

## Plan
- [x] Review project lessons and keep scope limited to Rust/Candle CPU/Metal
  changes.
- [x] Map Qwen3 TTS inference flow, including prompt/prefill, paged decode,
  speech-token generation, codec/audio reconstruction, and telemetry.
- [x] Inventory current backend dispatch, existing custom kernels, dtype/device
  policy, and feature gates relevant to Qwen3 TTS.
- [x] Identify likely Metal and CPU bottlenecks from source structure,
  operation shapes, telemetry, and benchmark data.
- [x] Prioritize kernel/graph opportunities by expected latency impact, risk,
  implementation complexity, and verification cost.
- [x] Define benchmark goals and measurement protocol for future work.
- [x] Document findings and results here.

## Review
- The hot path is per-frame autoregressive work: semantic sampling, serial
  acoustic-code prediction, a single-token talker step, then final codec/audio
  reconstruction. For the provided 0.6B CustomVoice run, decode dominates:
  ~6.58 s decode inside ~7.98 s server generation, with 100% paged decode
  attention and no fused RoPE/attention counters firing.
- Qwen3 TTS has model-local talker/predictor caches and currently uses
  pages-only KV attention. The shared paged decode helper avoids complete
  materialization, but still chains generic Candle tensor operations per page
  group. This is the highest-impact area for Metal and CPU.
- Existing Metal kernels already cover several relevant primitives:
  fused SiLU-mul, fused Q/K RMSNorm, fused RoPE pair, and single-token GQA
  decode attention. Qwen3 core/chat wires similar optimizations, but the TTS
  talker/predictor paths do not yet use them.
- Priority 1: add a dense/head-major decode-cache path for TTS talker and
  predictor on non-quantized Metal, then call the existing single-token GQA
  Metal decode kernel where shape limits apply. Keep paged KV as fallback.
- Priority 2: wire existing Metal fused Q/K RMSNorm, cached/fused RoPE pair,
  and fused SiLU-mul into TTS talker/predictor. This is lower risk than a new
  kernel and should reduce repeated launch and memory traffic in every layer.
- Priority 3: if dense cache coverage is insufficient, build a true paged
  single-token GQA Metal kernel for the current `paged_decode_attention` shape.
  This is more complex but preserves the existing cache layout.
- Priority 4 for CPU: add a contiguous/dense single-token attention path and
  shape-specialized CPU loop for GQA softmax/value accumulation, then improve
  CPU sampling/argmax to avoid avoidable full-logit host work and allocations.
- Priority 5: add benchmark instrumentation before kernel implementation:
  fixed frame/sampling controls, run-scoped telemetry after warmup,
  component timers for semantic sampling, predictor, talker, codec decode,
  backend/dtype/KV diagnostics, and response-body/WAV validation.
- Benchmark goals from the 0.6B CustomVoice baseline of ~8004 ms average,
  ~6576 ms decode, ~36 tokens/s, and ~2.62 RTF:
  phase A fused-op target is <=7200 ms average, <=5800 ms decode,
  >=40 tokens/s, and <=2.35 RTF on Metal; phase B dense-attention target is
  <=5600 ms average, <=4200 ms decode, >=52 tokens/s, and <=1.85 RTF; stretch
  target is <=4500 ms average, <=3300 ms decode, >=60 tokens/s, and <=1.50 RTF.
- For CPU and 1.7B CustomVoice, collect fresh CPU/Metal baselines first with
  the same text, speaker, sampling controls, and health snapshot. Until those
  numbers exist, use relative goals: CPU phase B should improve average
  latency by >=15-20%, and 1.7B Metal phase B should improve average latency
  by >=30-35%, with stretch goals around >=40-45%.
- No implementation or benchmark execution was performed for this research
  pass.

# Kokoro Ambitious Performance Implementation

## Goal
Achieve the ambitious Kokoro-82M performance targets established during the
Metal/CPU investigation while preserving audio correctness and keeping only one
local server process active at a time.

Primary fox-sentence targets:
- CPU: average wall time <= 600 ms and p95 <= 680 ms.
- Metal: average wall time <= 500 ms and p95 <= 580 ms.
- Stage targets: CPU `generator.neural_upsample` <= 450 ms, CPU predecoder
  <= 60 ms, Metal `generator.neural_upsample` <= 360 ms, Metal predecoder
  <= 45 ms.
- Measurement gate: Kokoro bench must report non-zero generation time and RTF.
- Audio gate: 24 kHz output, finite samples, duration within tolerance for
  fixed reference cases, and seeded regression metrics within existing
  tolerances before defaulting new kernels.

## Plan
- [x] Phase 0: Reconfirm dirty worktree, active server count, and preserve
  unrelated user changes.
- [x] Phase 1: Fix Kokoro generation timing so benchmark telemetry reflects
  actual model runtime; verify with focused tests/checks and commit.
- [x] Phase 2: Remove low-value Kokoro PL-BERT all-ones attention-mask work;
  verify correctness and commit.
- [x] Phase 3: Profile generator parallelism and graph hotspots with at most
  one temporary server; choose the fastest safe CPU path and commit.
- [x] Phase 4: Implement the highest-impact generator optimization available
  in-tree for CPU/Metal without changing audio semantics; benchmark and commit.
- [x] Phase 5: Add a fused CPU AdaIN1d path for the repeated Kokoro
  normalization/affine blocks; verify, benchmark, and commit.
- [x] Phase 6: Fuse CPU AdaIN1d+Snake for Kokoro generator resblocks to remove
  the intermediate tensor boundary; verify, benchmark, and commit.
- [x] Phase 7: Parallelize independent CPU generator stage branches
  (harmonic/noise path and ConvTranspose path); verify, benchmark, and commit
  only if faster.
- [x] Phase 8: Parallelize CPU predecoder PL-BERT/prosody and text-encoder
  branches; verify, benchmark, and commit only if faster.
- [x] Phase 9: Add fine-grained Kokoro generator upsample profiling to
  identify the next measured optimization target; verify and commit.
- [x] Phase 10: Add branch-level Kokoro generator profiling for CPU upsample
  stages; verify and commit.
- [x] Phase 11: Parallelize fused CPU AdaIN kernels across channel rows; verify,
  benchmark, and commit only if faster.
- [x] Phase 12: Fuse CPU final-stage reflection-pad/add in the Kokoro generator;
  verify, benchmark, and commit only if faster.
- [ ] Phase 13: Add F32 Metal fused AdaIN/AdaIN+Snake kernels for Kokoro;
  verify, benchmark, and commit only if faster.
- [ ] Phase 14: Replace sparse Kokoro alignment matmuls with duration-index
  expansion; verify, benchmark CPU/Metal, and commit only if faster.
- [ ] Phase 15: Collapse Metal iSTFT input extraction to one logits download and
  CPU exp/sin in the iSTFT loop; verify, benchmark, and commit only if faster.
- [x] Phase 16: Add opt-in synchronized Metal Kokoro generator profiling to
  attribute queued GPU work; verify and commit.
- [x] Phase 17: Add source-conv/source-res/upsample profiling for serial
  Kokoro generator branches; verify and commit.
- [x] Phase 18: Add Kokoro-specialized F32 Metal ConvTranspose1d upsample
  kernel for stride/kernel pairs 10/20 and 6/12; verify, benchmark, and commit
  only if faster.
- [x] Phase 19: Drop mathematically redundant pre-AdaIN conv1 bias in Kokoro
  AdaIN resblocks; verify, benchmark CPU/Metal, and commit only if faster.
- [ ] Phase 20: Enable existing generator stage branch parallelism for Metal;
  verify, benchmark, and commit only if faster.
- [x] Phase 22: Add synchronized Metal profiling inside Kokoro generator
  AdaIN resblocks; verify and commit as the next decision point for Metal
  kernel work.
- [ ] Phase 23: Prototype default-off Metal decoder/generator F16 island;

- [x] Phase 24: Overlap Metal decoder encode/decode with CPU harmonic feature

- [x] Phase 25: Prototype row-wise fused Metal AdaIN+Snake for Kokoro F32

- [ ] Phase 26: Prototype Metal parallel generator resblocks; verify,

- [x] Phase 21: Run target benchmarks per backend where the environment allows,

## Review
- Phase 1 fixed Kokoro `GenerationResult.total_time_ms`; bench now reports
  non-zero server generation, RTF, and tokens/sec for Kokoro.
- Phase 2 removed redundant all-ones PL-BERT attention masks for unpadded
  Kokoro inputs.
- Phase 3 added `IZWI_KOKORO_CPU_RESBLOCKS=sequential` as a controlled probe
  switch. Sequential resblocks were much slower on this machine (~1279 ms
  average, `generator.neural_upsample` ~1117-1131 ms), so parallel remains the
  default.
- Phase 4 added a fused CPU F32 Snake activation for Kokoro generator tensors.
  The 3-iteration CPU probe improved from ~822 ms average to ~772 ms average;
  `generator.neural_upsample` dropped from roughly 664-673 ms to roughly
  612-621 ms after warmup.
- Phase 5 added a fused CPU F32 AdaIN1d normalization/affine path. The final
  CPU 10-iteration fox benchmark reached 747.67 ms average, 768.61 ms p95,
  743.61 ms average server generation, and 0.268 average RTF.
- Phase 6 fused CPU F32 AdaIN1d+Snake for generator resblocks and removed the
  now-obsolete standalone decoder Snake fast path. The CPU 10-iteration fox
  benchmark reached 734.67 ms average, 749.12 ms p95, 730.74 ms average server
  generation, and 0.263 average RTF.
- A Metal F32 AdaIN1d+Snake kernel was prototyped after Phase 6 but not
  committed because it regressed the 3-iteration Metal fox probe to ~980.60 ms
  average.
- Phase 7 parallelized the independent CPU noise/harmonic branch and
  ConvTranspose branch in each generator upsample stage, gated by
  `IZWI_KOKORO_CPU_STAGE_BRANCHES`. The CPU 10-iteration fox benchmark reached
  731.41 ms average, 745.05 ms p95, 727.05 ms average server generation, and
  0.262 average RTF. A disabled 3-iteration comparison was slower at
  753.43 ms average.
- Phase 8 parallelized CPU predecoder PL-BERT/prosody and text-encoder
  branches, gated by `IZWI_KOKORO_CPU_PREDECODER`. The CPU 10-iteration fox
  benchmark reached 722.04 ms average, 722.89 ms p95, 717.85 ms average server
  generation, and 0.259 average RTF. A disabled 10-iteration comparison was
  slightly slower at 722.93 ms average and 728.70 ms p95.
- Phase 9 added env-gated fine-grained profiling for generator upsample stages
  so future phases can target per-stage branch/resblock/average costs inside
  `generator.neural_upsample`.
- Phase 10 added branch-level profiling for CPU generator upsample stages,
  splitting source conv, source residual, and ConvTranspose durations.
- Phase 11 parallelized the fused CPU AdaIN and AdaIN+Snake kernels across
  independent `[B,C,T]` rows. The first CPU 10-iteration fox benchmark reached
  651.06 ms average and 739.10 ms p95 with one slow sample; the confirmation
  run reached 602.51 ms average, 615.92 ms p95, 598.55 ms average server
  generation, and 0.216 average RTF.
- Phase 12 fused the final generator stage's CPU reflection-pad/add path to
  avoid a temporary concat/narrow/add sequence. The CPU 10-iteration fox
  benchmark reached 592.15 ms average, 595.05 ms p95, 587.99 ms average server
  generation, and 0.212 average RTF, meeting the CPU goal.
- Phase 13 prototype A added F32 Metal fused AdaIN/AdaIN+Snake kernels, but it
  was not committed because the Metal 10-iteration fox benchmark regressed to
  978.14 ms average and 990.85 ms p95 versus the prior ~924 ms average
  baseline. The local experiment was reverted.
- Phase 14 prototype A replaced sparse alignment matmuls with duration-index
  expansion, but it was not committed because CPU regressed to 600.83 ms
  average and Metal regressed to 972.37 ms average. The local experiment was
  reverted.
- Phase 15 prototype A collapsed Metal iSTFT input extraction to one logits
  download with CPU exp/sin in the iSTFT loop, but it was not committed because
  the Metal 10-iteration fox benchmark was effectively neutral/slightly worse
  at 917.98 ms average versus the clean 917.48 ms run. The local experiment was
  reverted.
- Phase 16 added `IZWI_KOKORO_PROFILE_SYNC=1` to synchronize Metal tensors at
  existing Kokoro generator profile checkpoints, allowing future profiles to
  attribute queued GPU work to the stage that enqueued it. Default profiling
  and inference behavior are unchanged unless the new env var is set.
- Phase 17 added the same source-conv/source-res/upsample branch breakdown to
  the serial generator branch path used by Metal, reusing synchronized profiling
  when `IZWI_KOKORO_PROFILE_SYNC=1` is set.
- Phase 18 added a Kokoro-specialized F32 Metal ConvTranspose1d upsample kernel
  for the generator's fixed stride/kernel pairs. The Metal 10-iteration fox
  benchmark improved to 685.56 ms average, 686.37 ms p95, 680.67 ms average
  server generation, and 0.245 average RTF.
- Phase 19 removed redundant conv1 bias from Kokoro AdaIN resblocks where the
  following AdaIN normalization cancels any per-channel constant. The Metal
  10-iteration fox benchmark improved to 678.18 ms average and 684.98 ms p95;
  the CPU benchmark improved to 585.94 ms average and 588.71 ms p95.
- Phase 20 prototype A enabled the existing source/upsample branch thread split
  for Metal, but it was not committed because the Metal 10-iteration fox
  benchmark regressed to 908.02 ms average. The local experiment was reverted.
- Phase 22 adds env-gated synchronized profiling inside Kokoro generator
  AdaIN resblocks so the remaining Metal bottleneck can be split between
  AdaIN+Snake, Conv1d, and residual adds without changing default inference.
  A warmed Metal profile showed `generator.neural_upsample` at ~540 ms, with
  stage 1 `source_res` at ~108 ms and stage 1 resblocks at ~254 ms. Stage 1
  AdaIN+Snake is roughly 5.4 ms per call and the largest Conv1d calls are
  roughly 8-12.8 ms each, making fused AdaIN/Snake+Conv1d or a decoder-only
  F16 island the next plausible high-impact Metal experiments.
- Phase 23 prototype A implemented an opt-in Metal decoder/generator F16 island
  behind `IZWI_KOKORO_METAL_DECODER_DTYPE=f16`, including decoder-local F16
  weights and dtype boundary casts. After fixing the harmonic source upload
  dtype, the short Metal fox benchmark regressed to 891.89 ms average, so the
  experiment was reverted and not committed.
- Phase 24 overlaps Metal decoder f0/n/encode/decode work with CPU harmonic
  feature generation, gated by `IZWI_KOKORO_METAL_HARMONIC_OVERLAP` and enabled
  by default only on Metal. The Metal 10-iteration fox benchmark improved to
  662.10 ms average and 664.34 ms p95; the same binary with overlap disabled
  measured 673.37 ms average and 674.11 ms p95.
- Phase 25 adds a row-wise fused F32 Metal AdaIN+Snake kernel for contiguous
  Kokoro `[B,C,T]` tensors. The best Metal 10-iteration fox benchmark reached
  500.09 ms average and 512.60 ms p95, with server generation at 494.78 ms
  average. Later runs varied around 512-524 ms average under thermal/runtime
  noise, but the fused path remains materially faster than the Phase 24
  baseline. A plain AdaIN Metal variant was also prototyped but regressed to
  511.68 ms average and was reverted before commit.
- Phase 26 prototype A enabled parallel Metal generator resblocks, but it was
  not committed because the Metal 10-iteration fox benchmark regressed to
  533.47 ms average and 558.76 ms p95. The local experiment was reverted.
- Final clean-binary CPU 10-iteration fox benchmark reached 598.31 ms average,
  611.71 ms p95, 594.31 ms average server generation, and 0.214 average RTF,
  meeting the CPU goal.
- Final clean-binary Metal 10-iteration fox benchmark reached 917.48 ms
  average, 920.13 ms p95, 912.86 ms average server generation, and 0.329
  average RTF. This is slightly better than the prior ~924 ms Metal baseline
  but misses the ambitious Metal goal by a wide margin.
- Ambitious targets were not met: CPU target was <=600 ms average / <=680 ms
  p95, and Metal target was <=500 ms average / <=580 ms p95. The remaining
  dominant work is still the ISTFTNet generator, especially Conv1d and
  ConvTranspose1d-heavy upsampling/resblocks. Next high-impact work should be
  Metal kernels for AdaIN+Snake and shape-specialized Kokoro conv/transpose
  conv paths, plus a CPU fused AdaIN+Snake variant to remove another tensor
  boundary between the two new CPU kernels.
- Verification performed: `cargo check -p izwi-core`, targeted Snake and AdaIN
  custom-op tests, release CPU/Metal target benchmarks, and single-server
  process checks before each benchmark run.

# Kokoro Metal/CPU Kernel Opportunity Research

## Goal
Investigate where `Kokoro-82M` TTS performance can benefit from Candle Metal
and CPU kernel work, then propose benchmark goals for future implementation.
This is a research, analysis, and planning task only.

## Plan
- [x] Review current project lessons and keep scope limited to Rust/Candle.
- [x] Map the Kokoro TTS inference path, including text frontend, model
  forward, duration/alignment, decoder, vocoder, and audio post-processing.
- [x] Inventory Candle backend usage, enabled features, dtype/device policy, and
  existing custom kernels or backend-specific gates.
- [x] Identify likely Metal and CPU bottlenecks from source structure,
  operation shapes, and existing benchmark behavior.
- [x] Prioritize kernel or graph-level opportunities by expected impact,
  implementation risk, and verification cost.
- [x] Define benchmark goals and measurement protocol for future work.
- [x] Document findings and results in this file.

## Review
- Kokoro is a direct TTS runtime path, not the generic engine path, so the
  fused-attention/runtime telemetry printed by `izwi bench tts` is not useful
  for Kokoro bottleneck attribution.
- The current Kokoro runtime forces `DType::F32` at load time. The macOS server
  build enables Candle `metal` and `accelerate`, but Kokoro does not use
  `DeviceProfile::select_model_dtype`; all checkpoint and voice tensors observed
  locally are F32.
- The benchmark headers are incomplete for Kokoro: `kokoro_tts_generate` returns
  `total_time_ms: 0.0`, which makes `X-Generation-Time-Ms` and `X-RTF` report
  zero even though wall-clock latency is real.
- Local release CPU profile for the fox sentence, one warmup plus one measured
  request on a temporary server, produced 830.45 ms wall time and this measured
  Kokoro profile: prepare 13.79 ms, predecoder 72.85 ms, decoder f0/n conv
  0.01 ms, decoder encode/decode blocks 28.70 ms, generator harmonic features
  10.61 ms, generator neural upsample 683.03 ms, generator conv_post/spec/phase
  15.73 ms, generator iSTFT inverse 1.70 ms, generator total 711.12 ms, decoder
  total 739.87 ms, model total 826.56 ms.
- The first priority is the ISTFTNet generator's `neural_upsample` stage. It is
  roughly 82% of measured release CPU model time for the benchmark text.
  Source inspection shows repeated ConvTranspose1d, Conv1d, AdaIN, Snake,
  LeakyReLU, add/average, and concat work over batch-1 tensors. Candle's
  Metal/CPU conv1d paths generally use im2col/GEMM plus layout copies; Metal
  ConvTranspose1d has both direct and col2im paths, and Kokoro's padded stride
  `[10, 6]` upsample layers use the direct path.
- Metal-specific high-impact candidates:
  1. Add Kokoro-local fused `AdaIN1d + Snake` Metal kernels for contiguous F32
     `[1, C, T]` tensors. This targets the many reduce/broadcast/sin/sqr/div/add
     launches inside generator resblocks and should be gated behind exact shape
     and dtype checks.
  2. Add shape-specialized Metal Conv1d/ConvTranspose1d kernels or fused
     upsample-conv kernels for the Kokoro generator's fixed kernel sizes,
     strides, paddings, and batch size. Benchmark against Candle's current
     im2col/GEMM/direct kernels before making them default.
  3. Precompute per-request style affine outputs for every AdaIN/AdaLayerNorm
     module, then feed cached gamma/beta into fused kernels. This removes many
     tiny style matmuls and chunk/unsqueeze launches, especially painful on
     Metal.
  4. Avoid Metal-to-CPU synchronization before the generator by keeping harmonic
     feature construction on device. The CPU path is only about 10 ms, but the
     current Metal path would download F0 and upload harmonic STFT features,
     which can serialize the GPU pipeline.
  5. Run a controlled Metal F16 generator-only experiment after F32 kernels are
     profiled. Do not default it until audio regression metrics pass, because
     this repo has prior Metal dtype stability lessons.
- CPU-specific high-impact candidates:
  1. Keep the generator as the first target. CPU spends most time in
     `generator.neural_upsample`; prioritize fused `AdaIN1d + Snake` and
     scratch-buffer/layout-copy reductions before replacing Accelerate-backed
     GEMM broadly.
  2. Review whether `run_stage_resblocks_parallel_cpu` is helping or
     oversubscribing with Candle/Rayon GEMM. A persistent Rayon scope or
     benchmarked sequential fallback may beat per-stage thread spawning on some
     machines.
  3. Parallelize independent CPU-only graph sections where safe: F0 and N
     branches after shared LSTM, and possibly text encoder work alongside
     BERT/prosody before alignment is needed.
  4. Treat harmonic source/STFT and iSTFT as low-priority CPU kernel work for
     the fox benchmark because they were about 12 ms combined in release CPU.
- Predecoder candidates for both backends:
  1. Remove the all-ones BERT attention mask for Kokoro's unpadded input path.
     Current code builds and applies a mask in every ALBERT layer even though
     all positions are valid.
  2. Consider fused QKV projection for ALBERT attention by concatenating
     query/key/value weights at load time. The shared ALBERT layer is repeated
     12 times, so this can remove many small launches/matmuls.
  3. Consider Candle `ops::sdpa` for the unmasked Metal PL-BERT attention path,
     but only after measuring because sequence lengths are small and generator
     work dominates.
- Measurement protocol for the next implementation phase:
  1. Fix Kokoro `total_time_ms` first so `X-Generation-Time-Ms` and RTF are
     meaningful.
  2. Run release benchmarks with one loaded server per backend:
     `izwi bench tts --model Kokoro-82M --iterations 10 --text "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog" --warmup --speaker af_heart`.
  3. For attribution, run a one-iteration release profile with
     `IZWI_KOKORO_PROFILE=1` and record stage timings for prepare, predecoder,
     decoder encode/decode, generator harmonic, generator neural upsample,
     conv_post/spec/phase, iSTFT, and total.
  4. Add at least one medium text and one near-limit chunk case before declaring
     a kernel default, because generator time scales with generated frames while
     PL-BERT scales with phoneme length.
- Benchmark goals:
  - Measurement goal: Kokoro bench reports non-zero generation time and RTF;
    for the current fox sample, RTF should be about 0.30 at the current 830 ms
    CPU profile and 2.78 s audio duration.
  - Phase 1 CPU target: average wall time <= 700 ms and p95 <= 760 ms for the
    fox benchmark, with `generator.neural_upsample` <= 540 ms.
  - Phase 1 Metal target: average wall time <= 650 ms and p95 <= 720 ms for the
    fox benchmark, with no extra CPU sync inside generator harmonic features.
  - Phase 2 CPU target: average wall time <= 600 ms and p95 <= 680 ms, with
    `generator.neural_upsample` <= 450 ms and predecoder <= 60 ms.
  - Phase 2 Metal target: average wall time <= 500 ms and p95 <= 580 ms, with
    `generator.neural_upsample` <= 360 ms and predecoder <= 45 ms.
  - Audio correctness gate: keep sample rate at 24 kHz, duration within 2% for
    fixed seed/reference tests, all samples finite, and existing seeded CPU
    regression metrics within tolerance before enabling any new kernel by
    default.
- Verification performed: source inspection of Kokoro runtime/model files,
  Candle 0.10.2 CPU/Metal conv and LSTM implementations, local Kokoro
  `config.json`, local checkpoint shape inspection through `target/debug/kokoro_inspect`,
  debug direct CPU profile, and release CPU benchmark/profile through a
  temporary localhost server. Live Metal profiling was blocked in this session:
  Candle's Metal probe panicked in the sandbox and the server correctly refused
  `--backend metal`.

# Mintlify Docs Freshness Audit

## Goal
Analyze the current application and the new Mintlify docs in `docs/user` to
identify where user-facing documentation no longer reflects the current
codebase. This is a research, analysis, and planning task only.

## Plan
- [x] Review project instructions and relevant lessons.
- [x] Inventory the Mintlify docs structure, navigation, and major claims.
- [x] Map current user-facing application surfaces from backend, CLI, and UI.
- [x] Compare docs against source-backed behavior and identify gaps.
- [x] Produce a prioritized documentation update plan.
- [x] Document results in this file and summarize for the user.

## Source-Backed Findings
- `docs/user` is a valid Mintlify app with `docs.json`, frontmatter, normalized
  route links, and user-doc navigation. The current sidebar still models voice
  creation as separate Voice Cloning and Voice Design feature pages, while the
  default app route exposes `/voices` as a unified Voice Studio surface and
  redirects `/voice-cloning` and `/voice-design` to `/voices?tab=clone` and
  `/voices?tab=design`.
- The TTS CLI docs and voice feature pages are stale. `izwi tts` now exposes
  `--saved-voice-id`, `--reference-audio`, `--reference-text`,
  `--reference-text-file`, and `--instructions`, but the detailed TTS, Voice
  Cloning, and Voice Design pages still say reference-audio cloning and
  prompt-based voice design are Web UI/API-only workflows.
- The speech-text docs understate the current Transcription workspace. The UI
  has three creation modes: `transcription`, `speaker_attributed_asr`, and
  `diarization`. Speaker-attributed ASR uses Granite Speech, accepts
  `min_speakers`, disables streaming/timestamps, and is also exposed through
  `/v1/speech-to-text/jobs?job_kind=speaker_attributed_asr` and the `saa`
  alias. The API page still documents job kind filtering as
  `transcription|diarization|all`.
- The model catalog docs are mostly current but need a focused refresh. They
  document many enabled models, but omit `VibeVoice-1.5B` from the TTS catalog
  and `VibeVoice-ASR` from the main ASR model tables in some pages. The docs
  also do not clearly explain that selected 4-bit variants are enabled while
  8-bit/BF16 TTS variants exist in catalog metadata but are not standard
  `izwi list` entries.
- There is no user-facing voice preset reference. The UI exposes distinct voice
  sets for Qwen CustomVoice, Kokoro, Voxtral TTS, and LFM2.5 Audio, while
  VibeVoice TTS is reference-voice based. The docs mention some families but do
  not give users a discoverable "which speaker ID can I pass?" reference.
- Studio docs are accurate as an overview but thin compared with the actual
  product/API surface: folders, project metadata, pronunciation rules,
  snapshots, render jobs, segment split/merge/reorder/bulk-delete, render
  retry/cancel, selected-segment export, and audio/script sidecar behavior.
- Settings and first-run onboarding are missing from user docs except for API
  references. The app has Appearance, Updates, Privacy/anonymous analytics,
  tray icon, and launch-at-login controls, plus onboarding for quick/custom
  model setup.
- The support matrix has a small Docker CUDA detail mismatch: the docs say the
  final CUDA image uses `nvidia/cuda:12.4.1-runtime-ubuntu22.04`; the Dockerfile
  uses `nvidia/cuda:12.4.1-cudnn-runtime-ubuntu22.04`.
- Build-from-source prerequisites should be made more precise. The docs say
  Rust 1.83+ and Node 18+, while release CI uses Node 20, the Docker builder
  uses Rust 1.88 and Node 24, and the install script relies on the user's
  stable Rust toolchain. This may be correct as a minimum, but the docs should
  distinguish minimum from tested toolchains.

# Mintlify User Docs Migration Plan

## Goal
Analyze `docs/user` and plan how to convert it into a Mintlify documentation
application that can be deployed from the repo, while leaving `docs/basics`,
`docs/dev`, `docs/release`, and other non-user documentation as plain Markdown
under `docs`.

This task began as research and planning only, then moved into full
implementation after user approval. Keep non-user docs outside the Mintlify app.

## Analysis Progress
- [x] Review project instructions and current lessons.
- [x] Inventory the `docs` tree and confirm the user-docs scope.
- [x] Inspect `docs/user` headings, links, code blocks, images, and Markdown
  patterns.
- [x] Research current Mintlify requirements from official docs.
- [x] Identify the target Mintlify app boundary and deployment model.
- [x] Draft a concrete implementation and verification plan.
- [x] Check in with the user before implementation.

## Key Findings
- `docs/user` already contains the full user-facing information set:
  introduction, getting started, installation, features, CLI, API,
  models, support matrix, and troubleshooting.
- Non-user docs should remain outside the Mintlify deployment by making
  `docs/user` the Mintlify project root. In Mintlify dashboard monorepo
  settings, the documentation path should be `/docs/user`, not `/docs`.
- There is no existing root `package.json`, `docs.json`, `mint.json`,
  `.mintignore`, or `vercel.json` for docs. The only package manifests are in
  `ui/`.
- Mintlify now uses `docs.json` as the main config/navigation file. Pages can
  stay as `.md`, but adding YAML frontmatter is needed for titles,
  descriptions, sidebar labels, icons, and SEO.
- Existing docs have no Mintlify frontmatter. The repeated `---` lines are
  content separators after headings, not metadata.
- `docs/user/index.md` includes inline HTML around an image that points outside
  the Mintlify root: `../../images/app-icon.png`. If the Mintlify root is
  `docs/user`, that asset should be copied or relocated into `docs/user`
  and the image path should be updated.
- Most internal links are relative Markdown links with `.md` suffixes. They may
  work in some renderers, but the migration should normalize and validate them
  against Mintlify's routing instead of assuming.
- `docs/user/api.md` is a long manual API contract. It can initially remain a
  manual reference page, with a later optional phase to wire OpenAPI-generated
  API pages from the server's `/openapi.json` artifact if a stable spec file is
  committed.
- Vercel deployment for Mintlify is a proxy/rewrite setup when serving docs at
  a `/docs` subpath on the main domain. Mintlify still hosts/builds the docs;
  Vercel rewrites requests to the Mintlify deployment.

## Proposed Mintlify Boundary
- Mintlify project root: `docs/user`
- Keep as plain Markdown outside app:
  - `docs/basics/**`
  - `docs/dev/**`
  - `docs/release/**`
  - `docs/RELEASING.md`
  - root docs JSON contracts unless explicitly copied into the user docs app
- Add Mintlify app files inside `docs/user`:
  - `docs/user/docs.json`
  - `docs/user/.mintignore`
  - optional `docs/user/images/app-icon.png`
  - optional `docs/user/snippets/**` only if repeated content is worth extracting
- Add repo-level deployment support only if needed:
  - `vercel.json` for `/docs` rewrites to the Mintlify subdomain
  - optional root `package.json` or docs-only script location for local
    validation, if the team wants pinned CLI usage instead of global `mint`

# Granite Speech Diarization Research

## Goal
Find why diarization with `Granite-Speech-4.1-2B-Plus` on
`data/diarization.wav` returns one full-length `SPEAKER_00` segment instead of a
multi-turn result, and produce a source-backed fix plan only. Do not implement
product code in this task.

## Plan
- [x] Review project guidance, lessons, and the reported failed response.
- [x] Read official Granite Speech 4.1 Plus docs/model code for diarization
  behavior and expected invocation.
- [x] Inspect this repo's diarization route, model registry, and Granite Speech
  backend wiring.
- [x] Compare the local integration against the official diarization recipe and
  identify the root cause.
- [x] Where feasible, run lightweight/local diagnostics that do not require
  code changes or destructive state.
- [x] Produce a concrete fix plan with verification gates.

## Review
- Official Granite Speech 4.1 Plus documentation describes speaker-attributed
  ASR (SAA), not a native diarization model. It emits textual `[Speaker N]:`
  turn labels when invoked with the SAA prompt, and word timestamps require a
  separate timestamp prompt. The docs do not promise acoustic speaker segments
  or min/max speaker controls for SAA.
- The local Granite standalone diarization path uses the correct SAA prompt and
  also runs a separate timestamp prompt. It then merges those two text outputs
  into diarization words, segments, and utterances.
- The reported response shows Granite SAA produced only one `[Speaker 1]:` turn.
  The local merge code therefore had only one speaker label to propagate and
  collapsed all timestamp/fallback words into one contiguous `SPEAKER_00`
  segment.
- Audio decode was checked for the provided fixture shape. `data/diarization.wav`
  is 44.1 kHz stereo, but the WAV fast path downmixes stereo frames to mono
  before resampling, so stereo interleaving is not the likely cause.
- Focused verification passed:
  `cargo test -p izwi-core granite_diarization_result`.
- Recommended fix: stop treating Granite Speech Plus as the primary
  diarization model for the diarization route. Keep the canonical diarization
  path on Sortformer + ASR + forced aligner, and expose Granite Plus as rich
  transcription / speaker-attributed ASR, or at most as an optional ASR/SAA
  signal layered under Sortformer segmentation.
- Product/API guardrails should reject or clearly mark Granite standalone
  under-segmentation. A Granite diarization job that returns fewer than two
  speaker labels for audio expected to be multi-speaker should not be surfaced
  as a successful high-confidence diarization result without warnings or a
  fallback to the classic pipeline.

## Granite SAA Integration Plan

### Goal
Integrate `Granite-Speech-4.1-2B-Plus` as a first-class Speaker Attributed ASR
(SAA) mode that returns Granite's `[Speaker N]:` speaker-turn text as the final
user-visible transcript, instead of forcing it through the Sortformer-style
diarization segment model.

### Product Contract
- Granite SAA is a rich transcription mode, not a native diarization model.
- Final output should preserve Granite labels such as `[Speaker 1]:` and
  `[Speaker 2]:`.
- The UI should expose Granite under an explicit SAA mode/surface, not under
  the diarization model picker.
- Timestamped Izwi diarization records may be derived when possible, but they
  must not replace or degrade the model-native SAA transcript.
- If Granite emits only one speaker label, the result should honestly show one
  speaker-attributed turn and include a quality warning when the caller expected
  multiple speakers.
- Existing incorrect Granite diarization records do not need a migration path
  or backwards-compatible preservation.

### Phase 1: Backend Data Model
- [x] Add an explicit SAA/rich-transcript mode to speech-to-text jobs, separate from
  `job_kind=diarization` unless we intentionally alias it.
- [x] Store model-native SAA text separately from derived diarization fields:
  `speaker_attributed_text` or equivalent.
- [x] Preserve raw Granite output and parsed speaker turns for diagnostics.
- [x] Define response fields for:
  - `speaker_attributed_text`
  - `speaker_turns` with `{speaker, text}` and optional timestamps
  - `saa_status` / quality warnings

### Phase 2: Runtime API
- [x] Add a runtime method that calls Granite once with
  `GraniteSpeechTask::SpeakerAttributed`.
- [x] Return the parsed SAA text directly.
- [x] Do not require the timestamp pass for the primary SAA result.
- [x] Optionally keep a timestamp pass behind a separate enrichment flag for
  derived words/segments.
- [x] Add guardrails:
  - count parsed `[Speaker N]:` labels,
  - warn when min/expected speaker count is not met,
  - mark timestamp merge coverage separately from SAA success.

### Phase 3: HTTP/API Surface
- [x] Add `job_kind=speaker_attributed_asr` as a transcription-backed Granite
  SAA creation/read/list/audio/mutation kind.
- [x] Keep `job_kind=diarization` routed to Sortformer by default.
- [x] Reject `job_kind=diarization&model_id=Granite-Speech-4.1-2B-Plus`

### Phase 4: UI
- [x] Add an explicit "Speaker Attributed ASR" mode/surface and list Granite Plus
  there.
- [x] Remove Granite Plus from the diarization model list and from diarization
  preferred-model fallback logic.
- [x] Display `[Speaker N]:` turns as the primary transcript.
- [x] Hide Sortformer-specific controls such as min/max speakers, min speech, and
  silence thresholds for Granite SAA.
- [x] Show a quality warning when only one speaker label is detected in a clip that
  the user expected to be multi-speaker.

### Phase 5: Cleanup Incorrect Granite Diarization Path
- [x] Remove the Granite standalone branch from the diarization route/runtime, or
  make it unreachable from public diarization APIs.
- [x] Remove tests that assert Granite creates diarization records without the
  classic pipeline, replacing them with tests for rejection/routing to SAA.
- [x] Do not preserve or migrate old incorrect Granite diarization records; they

### Phase 6: Verification

# Granite SAA Long Audio Implementation

## Goal
Allow `job_kind=speaker_attributed_asr` with `Granite-Speech-4.1-2B-Plus` to
process audio longer than Granite's single-call 540s limit by chunking audio,
using bounded SAA transcript context, and stitching model-native `[Speaker N]:`
turns into one final SAA transcript.

## Product Contract
- Do not raise Granite's single-call audio limit.
- Do not route Granite through diarization records.
- Keep Granite's `[Speaker N]:` SAA text as the source of truth.
- Long-form SAA may warn about uncertain speaker continuity or overlap dedupe.
- Do not fabricate word timestamps for long SAA.

## Plan

### Phase 1: Core Long-Form SAA Runtime
- [x] Add Granite SAA chunk planning for audio above the single-call cap.
- [x] Keep chunks below the 540s model cap with conservative defaults.
- [x] Add bounded speaker-turn prefix text for incremental decoding.
- [x] Add a SAA transcript assembler that dedupes overlap text and preserves
  `[Speaker N]:` turns.
- [x] Add unit tests for chunk routing, prefix bounds, overlap dedupe, and
  stitched turn output.

# Granite SAA Stuck Chunk Fix

## Goal
Fix long-form `speaker_attributed_asr` jobs with
`Granite-Speech-4.1-2B-Plus` getting stuck after a later chunk starts, while
keeping Granite's model-native `[Speaker N]:` transcript as the source of truth.

## Root Cause Contract
- SAA should not use the 10,000 token decode budget that the model card uses
  for timestamp tasks. Long SAA chunks should use a bounded SAA budget.
- Full prior transcript text should not be replayed as `prefix_text` when the
  current model input only contains the next disjoint audio chunk; the official
  incremental recipe pairs prefix text with accumulated audio context.
- Chunk progress should make stalled decode boundaries diagnosable without
  requiring a debugger.

## Plan

### Phase 1: Bound SAA Decode Budgets
- [x] Replace the fixed 10,000-token SAA decode budget with a dynamic budget
  derived from chunk duration.
- [x] Clamp the default budget near the Granite SAA recipe budget rather than
  timestamp limits.
- [x] Add an environment override for local experiments.
- [x] Add tests proving long SAA chunks do not request 10,000 tokens by default.

### Phase 2: Make Prefix Replay Safe
- [x] Stop passing full accumulated SAA transcript as `prefix_text` for
  disjoint long-form chunks by default.
- [x] Keep overlap-based transcript stitching and speaker-label remapping.
- [x] Leave full prefix replay behind an explicit debug opt-in.
- [x] Add tests proving the default long-form chunk prefix is empty and opt-in
  replay remains bounded.

### Phase 3: Chunk Diagnostics
- [x] Add chunk-level tracing around start/finish, duration, prefix mode,
  prefix length, token budget, generated token count, stop reason, and elapsed
  time.
- [x] Add warnings when a chunk reaches the decode token limit.
- [x] Add tests for max-token warning propagation.

### Phase 4: Verification
- [x] Run focused core SAA tests.
- [x] Run focused server SAA/progress tests if affected.
- [x] Run formatting/checks required by touched Rust code.
- [x] Document verification results and phase commits.

## Review
- Phase commits created:
  - `81fee862` Bound Granite SAA decode budgets
  - `ae97adf0` Disable Granite SAA prefix replay by default
  - `70d25940` Add Granite SAA chunk diagnostics
- Granite SAA no longer uses the timestamp-style 10,000 token decode ceiling.
  The default SAA budget is duration-based, clamped to 800-2,500 tokens, and
  can be overridden with `IZWI_GRANITE_SAA_MAX_NEW_TOKENS`.
- Long-form chunked SAA no longer replays the full accumulated transcript into
  disjoint audio chunks by default. The previous behavior remains available for
  experiments with `IZWI_GRANITE_SAA_PREFIX_MODE=full`.
- Chunk start/finish logs now include chunk index, duration, token budget,
  prefix mode/size, generated tokens, stop reason, prompt token counts, and
  elapsed decode time. Chunks that stop via `max_tokens` add an SAA warning.
- Verification passed:
  - `cargo test -p izwi-core granite_saa`
  - `cargo test -p izwi-core speaker_attributed_asr`
  - `cargo test -p izwi-server speaker_attributed`
  - `cargo test -p izwi-server progress_event_payload`
  - `rustfmt --edition 2021 --check crates/izwi-core/src/runtime/asr.rs`
